segments.text: 1. The Nest. Zero Minutes. Before the light has fully made up its mind about Onipa, the nest is already awake. Which is the great privilege of an open newsroom where nobody hides behind a door and every desk, including those belonging to people who are supposed to be working harder than I am, sits in plain view of mine. And this morning, the whole room is humming over one question, written on a sticky note in a pen pressed so hard it nearly tore the paper.
Why is Ghana a powerful nation?

Chale, how de ting de go? I am Kofi, the editor. This is the Gold Coast Pallava. And before the headlines, I owe you the price of this edition, because every paper has one and, de ting bise, we all know de hold, so ours is paid in data.
About 70 megabytes, the figure you see stamped on the screen, which is a fair fee for a story that took 77 years to unfold and an empire much longer to forgive.
If it accost you data, soak the story well, make it sweet you.
2. Front Page. 050.
Page 1 is always a mixed bag. So make we start.
And you will notice that every headline is a question, because the answers live on the inside pages, and the editor is a firm believer in suspense.
Our lead this edition.
What happened on the 22nd of January, 1824, when a British governor faced 10,000 Asante warriors and decided the correct reply was a brass band?
How did 50,000 ounces of gold, promised in 1874, become the excuse for an invasion 22 years later?
Why did a governor's complaint about his chair, in March of 1900, set a country on fire?
And, tucked in the corner like a classified ad, what object did an empire search for across the Asante forest, dig for under village huts, and never once managed to hold?
3. Lead Story. 150.
Do you remember the question at the top of page 1, about a governor who answered 10,000 warriors with a brass band?
That was the Battle of Nsamanko, fought on the 22nd of January, 1824, beside the Bonsar River, where the British governor, Sir Charles McCarthy, was killed along with much of his command,
and which Stephen Manning, the author of Britain at War with the Asante Nation, 1823-1900, The White Man's Grave,
which is our reference material, calls the high point of Asante prestige, power, and reach.
But to see why Ghana is powerful, you have to see what stood behind that day.
And that begins with a coastline so rich that foreigners named it after its gold,
and so crowded that of roughly 110 European forts built along the whole of West Africa, about 100 stood on this one stretch.
Elmina Castle, raised by the Portuguese in 1482, is still the oldest European building in tropical Africa.
Behind that shoreline, in a forest Europeans did not dare enter until the 19th century,
lived a people who are said to have taken their name from the red clay, asan.
They paid in tribute to the denchira, the asantefo, the clay diggers,
and who decided that they would be Nogodi's tributary again.
The first thing a junior high design class taught me, long before I understood why it mattered,
is that a good symbol can carry more weight than a building.
And the proof sits at the center of this story.
The priest Okonfu Anoche and the first king, Oseitutu, understood around 1701
that 24 proud and quarrelsome states would never fight as one because of a law.
So, according to Asante tradition, Anoche called a golden stool down from the sky
onto the lap of Oseitutu and declared that it held the spirit of the whole nation.
Ntim Jakari of the denchira was beaten at Fease that same year.
And Asante man stepped onto the map with a spirit that could not be taxed, bribed, or shot.
The second ingredient I appreciate from my senior high years of technical drawing and building construction,
where a design is only as good as the logistics beneath it.
The Asante army was a quota system,
each state sending a share of its men while the rest stayed home to farm.
So the nation fought without starving itself.
It marched in the shape of an ant column, with scouts, an advance guard,
a main body guarding the commander, two wings, and a home guard.
And uniquely among African armies, it carried a medical corps, the Esumangkwafo,
that treated the wounded and removed the dead,
partly from care and partly so the enemy could never count its losses.
The third belongs to my year of live and studio sound,
because the Asante knew that a drum in a forest is a weapon.
And at Nsamangkw, the battle I opened with,
Governor McCarthy, with about 500 men in his firing line,
faced something like 10,000 warriors
and ordered his band to play the British National Anthem,
evidently convinced that the sound of home would make them surrender.
Each time the anthem ended, the drums returned louder,
until the Asante tired of the performance and answered with musket fire.
The one storesman who struggled in with ammunition boxes found,
when they were opened, that they held biscuits and macaroni,
and McCarthy did not survive the afternoon.
While in Kumasi, the Asante king Osei Bonsu died in his bed the same day,
leaving his brother to inherit the greatest victory of the age.
Power is not invincibility, though.
And on Monday, the 7th of August, 1826,
the Asante were beaten at Dodoa by a coalition of British and Danish troops,
coastal militias, and the Achem, Denchira, and Akim.
Among them, the Achem queen Nana'afia Dukwa,
the only woman commander on the field,
who had drawn them onto open ground where drums and forest could not help them,
while Congreve rockets that the Asante took for a new kind of thunder and lightning
broke their line.
A lesser nation would have folded.
The Asante paid an indemnity of 4,000 ounces of gold and rebuilt.
And in 1874, about 40,000 of its warriors were in the field against Sir Garnet Wolseley,
who fought them at a moirful on the 31st of January
and dashed for Kumasi with four days of rations,
entering on the 4th of February,
after which 59 in every hundred of his 2,500 British soldiers
were killed, wounded, or invalided home.
The king had left.
Nobody remained to sign a peace.
And the Treaty of Fomenna, ratified in March after Wolseley had sailed,
demanded 50,000 ounces of gold that were never fully paid.
It'll be a small thing, because a debt, as your question card hinted, is a doorway.
In January 1896, a bloodless British force walked into Kumasi,
and King Prempe I and his chiefs, none of whom had ever seen the sea,
were pushed into a boat, held at Elmina for a year,
and sent on to Sierra Leone and the Seychelles.
And Manning reads Chamberlain's aim as less humanitarian than a race to beat the French to the interior.
4. The Wire, 620
On the afternoon of Wednesday, 28 March 1900,
Governor Sir Frederick Hodgson, who had left Accra on the 13th with an escort of only 30 Hauser soldiers,
and his wife, Lady Mary Alice, who was to be the first European woman to enter Kumasi,
stepped out of the fort in a uniform that dripped with gold braid,
and sat under an awning to address the kings and chiefs arranged in a semicircle in strict order of seniority.
He reminded them that the indemnity of 1874 was unpaid,
that Prempe would never return, and that they would supply labour for roads.
And then he asked why he had been given an ordinary chair,
when, as the queen's representative, he should have been brought the golden stool to sit on.
It was as if he had asked to sit on the nation's soul, because the stool is never sat upon,
and when Ya Asantewa, queen mother of Ajisu and its acting chief since the chief had been exiled with Prempe,
the only Asante woman present, asked about the king and was told again that he would not return,
she answered with words Asante tradition remembers as a declaration of war.
Tomorrow, ghost widows would get husbands.
That night, she led the chiefs in a secret meeting, and most agreed to defend the stool,
though some held back for fear of putting it at risk.
Hodgson's own notes to Chamberlain record the question about the chair,
and although Lady Hodgson's memoir denies he said it, the evidence is stacked against her.
Three days later, on the 31st, Captain Armitage and 45 Hausa soldiers followed a boy named Esumi into the bush
and dug under hut floors for a stool that was not there, returning to find an angry crowd waiting.
The fort was besieged until the 15th of July,
and Ya Asantewa and 14 others were sent to the Seychelles to join Prempe,
but the one thing Britain wanted never came into its hands.
The Asante had picked their moment well, because that season,
Britain was locked in a bitter war with the Boers in South Africa,
where Mafeking was not relieved until the 17th of May under Robert Baden-Powell,
the same man who had led the scouts on the march to Kumasi four years earlier.
And by June, the foreign legations in Peking were under siege as well,
so no British troops could be spared for what London saw as an obscure little outpost.
Manning argues that the siege of Kumasi fort deserves to stand beside Ladysmith and Peking.
5. The Pallava Desk, 825
A Pallava Desk should be uncomfortable,
so I will put two truths on the table and refuse to remove either.
The first is that Asante expansion, as Manning plainly writes,
was driven largely by the demand for captives to sell,
that human sacrifice was real, and that a nation can be powerful and still do things we would not defend today.
The second is that talk of humanitarian duty was a convenient costume for a scramble,
and that the Fante, Achim, Tenchira and other southern peoples,
who had their own reasons to fear Kumasi, fought beside the British more than once.
This was never one hero and one villain.
It was a neighbourhood argument an empire learned to exploit.
Wahaladeh everywhere.
Power and virtue are different things,
and the honest thing is to hold the pride and the cost in the same hand.
6. Then vs Now, 935
Then, a defeated king owed an empire 50,000 ounces of gold.
Now, this June, at a conference in Accra,
the Netherlands handed over a catalogue of about 2,000 objects it plans to return.
Germany named its first items,
Denmark pledged to help preserve Christiansborg Castle as a place of remembrance,
and the 32 Asante treasures that came home from London in 2024
sit on an initial three-year loan, renewable once.
So the argument over who owns the story, and the gold, is still alive.
In 2027, Ghana turned 70 on the 6th of March,
and in Kumasi, the Asante flag still flies beside the national one,
which is how you can tell that the stool never changed hands.
Between then and now runs a thread.
Asante was annexed in 1901, yet governed separately.
Prempe returned in 1925.
A successor was restored as Asantehene in 1935,
and the Gold Coast Regiment that grew out of these wars fought in Burma and Abyssinia,
whose veterans, whom my grandfather is one of,
came home to unpaid pensions and the jobs they had been promised,
grievances that exploded at a crossroads in Accra in February 1948.
7. The Team Aside
Back at the Nest, there is a young man named Kwame,
whom the Nest has already decided to call The Combative,
who prepared for this edition the way others prepare for a boxing match,
arriving with a sheet of paper that said
BRITAN WON in capital letters,
and when I said TIKKOM and held out my hand for it,
he gave it to me like a man handing over a trophy,
defending it with two facts.
Kumasi was taken in 1874,
and Prempe was exiled in 1896.
He had a point,
and I let him keep it until I asked one question about the golden stool,
though when he began gloating,
I told him, with a smile,
KUMOT FODE
His keyboard stopped,
his chin lifted,
and he asked, very quietly,
whether the British ever found it.
And when I said no,
the look on his face said the TING PIN MIU,
and he folded the paper in half and did not unfold it again.
I will tell you more about Kwame in good time.
The Editor's Note
You may have noticed that I keep stepping out of the history into other rooms,
a design class here,
a studio there,
and that is the reason I sit in the editor's chair at all,
because I did things in the wrong order,
on purpose.
I began with drawing and design,
spent a year in visual art,
and swerved into the technical program,
physics,
elective maths,
building construction,
and technical drawing,
where I learned that every grand idea is only a drawing
until someone works out how to hold it up.
Between school and college,
I took a year to learn sound,
live and studio,
while working as a medic in a clinic,
which taught me in the same 12 months
how a room listens and how a body fails.
Then, I read psychology and philosophy,
became hands-on with every new technology I could find,
and worked for an electronic security systems company,
where I learned that the best system is the one nobody can find,
a lesson the golden stool taught an empire at great cost.
All the while,
I kept one eye on football,
and one on the wider world,
and I ended up in broadcasting and writing,
because I have never been able to refuse an adventure.
Everything in this edition,
the symbol,
the logistics,
the sound,
the secrecy,
and the nation's mind,
I met first in some other room.
And that,
I think,
is what an editor is for.
Not to know one thing,
but to know where the ideas are hiding.
The letters page,
Letters page.
And this week's question is one of recall.
Of everything you heard in this edition,
which single detail will you repeat to someone tomorrow?
And who is that someone?
Write it in the comments,
I will pin the best one,
and the strongest letters will be read in the next edition.
The Dispatch,
That is the first edition of the Gold Coast Palava.
Complete,
checked,
stamped,
priced at about 70 megabytes,
filed and signed at the Nest 266 Sandpiper Loop,
Onipa Enclave,
and dispatched to Accra,
to Kumasi,
to Bungpurugu,
to Half Asini,
and to the world.
Chale,
I go see you for the next one.
